The social sciences are kind of strict when it comes to this sort of thing. The only time it seems permissible to speculate is in the discussion of a journal article. Elsewhere it falls victim to criticism and cynicism. You either have supporting data to back your claims or you stay silent to prevent the spread of misinformation and pseudoscience.

In that regard, I think it makes casual discussion a bit strained, yeah?
Does speculation have a place in Criminology?
I believe that locking out uhm ... ways of thinking ... generally is bad, because it also locks out all the new ideas and considerations that might prove to be valueable for progress.
Hmmm. I guess speculation does allow for the creation of research questions and theories that bind similar studies together.

If by speculation you mean criminal philosophy (ex. This may be why x occurs), then I would have to say yes. We can have a discussion based on our own personal philosophies that could explain the motive and thus by doing so influence the newest line of research into using the scientific method to prove or deny our speculations.

It would be hard to actively engage in conversation in Criminology without a little speculation. I engage in speculation all the time when I comment on crime articles. Mostly what I do is parrot the lessons that I've learned in university. Most of the time I do so without making direct reference to any study. If we were to have to base everything we say upon direct scientific evidence, I don't think we'd have much to talk about.
